summary: Specifies how to set up and maintain pseudowires, which emulate Layer 2 services such as Frame Relay, ATM and Ethernet over an MPLS network, using extensions to the Label Distribution Protocol (LDP). Encapsulation details are in companion documents. It is a proposed standard. It was replaced by RFC 8077.

plainLanguage.summary: A pseudowire carries a Layer 2 service across an MPLS network. RFC 4447 explains how the two edge routers use LDP to agree on labels, identify the pseudowire and report its status.

questions: how to signal pseudowires over mpls
how does ldp set up a pseudowire
what is the pwid fec element
subtitle: How edge routers use LDP to set up and maintain point-to-point pseudowires over MPLS.

tldr.problem: Two edge routers need to identify the same pseudowire so they can carry an emulated Layer 2 service across an MPLS network.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4447 extends LDP with FEC elements, labels, parameters and status signaling that bind an MPLS label to a pseudowire.
tldr.outcome: RFC 4447 has been obsoleted by RFC 8077 and was updated by RFCs 6723, 6870 and 7358.

today: RFC 4447 has been obsoleted by RFC 8077. It was also updated by RFC 6723, RFC 6870 and RFC 7358.

sections.title: Pseudowires Carry Layer 2 Services
sections.content:
A pseudowire emulates a Layer 2 service such as Frame Relay, ATM or Ethernet across an MPLS-enabled network. Companion documents define how the Layer 2 units are encapsulated; RFC 4447 defines how endpoints establish and maintain the pseudowire.

The RFC covers point-to-point pseudowires. It uses the term provider edge (PE) for the routers at the two ends and calls the local customer connection an attachment circuit.
sections.plainLanguage: A pseudowire connects two edge routers and carries an emulated Layer 2 service between them. This RFC covers how those routers establish and maintain that connection.

sections.title: The Pseudowire Label
sections.content:
The MPLS label used as the pseudowire demultiplexor is called the PW label. The sending PE adds it to the packet; if the packet also travels through an MPLS tunnel, the tunnel label is pushed above it.

At the far PE, the PW label identifies the pseudowire and helps the router choose the outgoing interface and service-specific identifier. The core can carry many pseudowires through a tunnel without keeping per-pseudowire state.
sections.plainLanguage: The sending edge router adds a label that identifies the pseudowire. The receiving edge router reads that label to choose where to deliver the Layer 2 data.

sections.title: Identifying a Pseudowire with LDP
sections.content:
LDP carries a FEC element that identifies the pseudowire along with its label. The PWid FEC element, type 0x80, is used when both endpoints have the same provisioned 32-bit identifier. It includes the PW type, Group ID, PW ID and optional interface parameters.

The Generalized PWid FEC element, type 0x81, identifies the attachment group and the source and target attachment identifiers. The two directions of a bidirectional pseudowire use corresponding LDP mappings with the source and target identifiers reversed.
sections.plainLanguage: LDP can identify a pseudowire with one shared numeric ID or with identifiers for its two endpoints. The routers use that information to match the labels to the same service.

sections.title: Reporting Pseudowire Status
sections.content:
When a pseudowire is configured and enabled, the PEs send Label Mapping messages even if an attachment circuit is inactive. A PW Status TLV can report faults without withdrawing the label; it contains a 4-octet status code whose bits can report more than one fault.

The endpoints negotiate whether to use the PW Status TLV when the pseudowire is first set up. If the remote PE does not support it, the endpoints fall back to using label withdrawal to signal status.
sections.plainLanguage: The edge routers can tell each other when a pseudowire has a fault while keeping its label binding in place. If they cannot use the status message, they use label withdrawal instead.

sections.title: Protecting Data and LDP Signaling
sections.content:
The RFC separates security for the carried data from security for LDP control messages. A pseudowire's encapsulation does not itself authenticate the sender, protect data from alteration or provide privacy, so the MPLS network needs controls against unauthorized packet insertion and access.

An LDP session must be accepted only from an eligible peer, and source-address spoofing must be prevented. The RFC requires support for LDP MD5 authentication and says it should be used; it provides message integrity and authentication, but not privacy.
sections.plainLanguage: The pseudowire format alone does not prove who sent a packet or keep its contents private. The routers also need to restrict which peers can establish LDP sessions and protect those messages.
